title: The flower sermon
hookLine: the Buddha holds up a flower in silence; only Mahakassapa smiles, as Zen tells it (Gateless Gate 6)

lines: ONE SMALL SMILE IN THE CAR.
cards: Some of the most important things that pass between two people happen without words. A look across a room when someone says something ridiculous, and you both know.
A parent and a teenager in the car, and one small smile that means, we're okay. A best friend who hands you a coffee before you've said a thing. Nobody explained anything, and everything got across.
Zen has a founding story built on that kind of moment: a huge crowd, the Buddha, and a sermon with no words at all.

teach.b: The Gateless Gate tells it in case six. The Buddha was on Vulture Peak, the mountain where he often taught, with a great assembly gathered to hear him. He didn't speak.
He held up a flower. Everyone was silent, waiting, puzzled.
Only Mahakassapa, one of his senior disciples, broke into a smile. Then the Buddha spoke.
He said, in effect: I have the treasury of the true teaching, the wondrous mind of nirvana, a gate that doesn't depend on words, a transmission outside the scriptures. I entrust it to Mahakassapa.

For Zen this is a beginning: the first link in the chain of teachers, mind to mind, that Zen traces from the Buddha through Mahakassapa to Bodhidharma, who brought it to China, to Huineng from yesterday, and on to teachers today.
This story isn't found in any early Indian text. It first shows up in Chinese Chan writings around the eleventh century, well over a thousand years after the Buddha.
Zen tells it as Zen's own story, and many Zen teachers say so openly; the Gateless Gate itself even teases the Buddha for it.

Mahakassapa is real in the older texts: in the Pali canon he's a strict forest-dwelling monk who, after the Buddha's death, leads the first gathering to recite the teachings. So the flower sermon is what Zen hears in him.
Its point stands whether or not you read it as history: some things are received, not explained. The flower was held up.

how: Zen schools tell the flower sermon as the start of their lineage, naming Mahakassapa as the first ancestor after the Buddha, and recite the names of the ancestors from the Buddha onward in their services.

games.q: you're in the crowd on Vulture Peak. the Buddha holds up a flower and says nothing. what happens next, as Zen tells it?
games.why: only Mahakassapa smiled, and the Buddha said he entrusted the teaching beyond words to him.

practice: If there's a flower or a leaf near you, pick it up; if not, a pen, a spoon or a stone will do. Hold it up in silence, without naming or describing it, and just look, the way the assembly on Vulture Peak looked.
If something in you softens, if a smile comes, let it come; if not, keep looking, then lower your hands and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Mahakassapa. The disciple who alone smiled when the Buddha held up a flower in silence: Zen's story of teaching passed mind to mind.

orig.note: Chinese niān huā wēi xiào: holding a flower, a faint smile, the name for this story.

carryVoice: Your line: the smile. Mind to mind, without a word. That's day two hundred eighty-three.
